swap.evidence: Products: a council parking-permit application and a campsite pitch booking. Survives unchanged: page ground, header/footer bands, single left column, bold labels over native inputs, petrol-blue rectangular button, red 'There is a problem' error summary, label/value review list, bordered radio cards. Bound to this product: only the words (sill gate, HW, pontoon, draught, MMSI), the tide table content and the anchor glyph. With the name and copy hidden, a reader could not tell this is for a tidal harbour.

category_guess.evidence: Predicted default for a small public-facing booking form: government-style single-column form, native controls, one dark accent on the primary button, red error summary, white/very light ground, no imagery. Predicted opposite: a glossy marina/yachting look with sea photography and navy-and-white nautical styling. The render matches the default on every identity-carrying element (root/default 1280 and 375; berths/default; review/default).

similar_prompt.evidence: Similar brief: 'online booking of pitches at a small municipal campsite; operate mode; mostly phones outdoors'. Predicted choices: the same accessible single-column form pattern, a dark single accent, error summary, summary list, bordered radio cards. Overlap: the whole visual layer. The brief's distinguishing fact — arrival is bounded by the sill-gate window around high water — never shapes the design; the arrival-time field is a plain select unrelated to the tide table and the gate rule is a grey footnote.

findings.title: The tide and sill-gate window, the product's defining mechanism, has no visual form
findings.description: The one fact that distinguishes this booking from any marina form — boats can only cross the sill about two hours either side of high water — appears only as body copy, a stock tide table below the form and a grey footnote. The arrival-time select is not visibly connected to the gate window, and no later step (berths, review, confirmation) shows the window for the chosen day.
findings.impact: Skippers new to the harbour may pick an arrival time outside the gate window because nothing in the form shows it; the design also has no element a visitor would recognise as belonging to this harbour.

evidence.detail: arrival-time select at y~465; gate rule as grey footnote at y~1060
tide table sits below the button; gate window never meets the time choice

findings.recommendation: Decide how the gate window for the chosen day becomes the organising element of the arrival step and recurs (review, confirmation), so the signature comes from the harbour's own mechanism rather than ornament.

findings.title: Wide viewports leave the right half empty and short pages end in an empty band below the footer
findings.description: At 1280 and 1440 all content sits in a ~540px left column with the right half of the viewport empty grey; on boat, review, confirmed and length-over-limit the footer ends part-way down and the page ground continues below it.
findings.impact: The page is likely to read as unfinished on desktop, where staff and planning skippers use it; the floating footer looks like a rendering fault.
findings.recommendation: Decide what the wide layout is for (e.g. whether reference material such as the tide window belongs beside the form) and make the page frame fill the viewport on short pages.

findings.title: Arrival date uses the unstyled browser date control showing yyyy/mm/dd
findings.description: The first field on the first page is the browser-default date input with placeholder 'yyyy/mm/dd' and a system calendar glyph, while the product formats dates as 'Saturday 17 October 2026' everywhere else.
findings.impact: It is the first thing a visitor touches; the year-first format contradicts the en-GB convention and may cause day/month slips, and the default look is a visible sign of unfinish.
findings.recommendation: Decide the date-entry pattern that matches the declared en-GB format on desktop as well as mobile, and give it the same visual treatment as the other fields.

findings.title: 'Change dates' is hidden in an orphaned overflow menu on the berth step
findings.description: On choose-berth a lone '...' button sits at the far right of the container, outside the form column, with a blank band to its left; it holds 'Change dates' and 'Harbour rules'.
findings.impact: Changing the arrival date is a core task; behind an unlabelled icon it is likely to be missed, and the isolated button pulls the eye away from the berth list at 1280.
findings.recommendation: Decide where the arrival summary and the way to change it live so they read as one unit in the content column.

findings.title: Tide table headers misaligned with figures, and times given in UTC
findings.description: 'Morning' and 'Afternoon' headers are left-aligned while the times below are right-aligned, so each header sits well left of its numbers; the caption says 'times in UTC' while the context sets 24-hour local times (17 October is in BST, one hour off).
findings.impact: Skippers planning a gate crossing may misread which column a time belongs to at a glance, and may be an hour out if they read UTC as local time.

evidence.detail: header 'Morning' at x~392 over times ending at x~515

findings.recommendation: Align headers with their figures and decide which time base skippers need, stated consistently with the arrival-time field.

findings.title: Invalid fields are marked inconsistently in error states
findings.description: In boat/errors the 'Length' input keeps a dark border while the three other invalid inputs are red; in review/errors 'Skipper's name' keeps a dark border while 'Mobile number' is red. Both have inline error messages.
findings.impact: Skippers scanning for what to fix may skip the field that does not look invalid. (May be a focus or hover artefact of the capture; stills cannot tell.)
findings.recommendation: Decide one invalid-field treatment that holds in every interaction state, including focus.

findings.title: 'Booking stopped' state is a bare dead end
findings.description: When the boat is over the berth's length limit the page shows only 'Booking stopped' and 'This booking cannot continue. Reference BK-409.' — no reason, no way back to choose a larger berth (the wall berth takes up to 15 m), no call to the office beyond the footer.
findings.impact: A skipper whose boat is too long for the chosen pontoon is likely to abandon the booking although a fitting berth exists; the page looks unfinished.
findings.recommendation: Decide what this state must tell the skipper (why, and which berths fit) and give it a next step.

findings.title: Confirmation omits the arrival time and the gate window
findings.description: The confirmation lists Arrival (date only), Berth and Nights. The arrival time chosen on step 1 (15:00), which the review page showed, and the gate window for that day are absent; the page is otherwise three rows and a link.
findings.impact: The page skippers keep 'to hand when you arrive' drops the one detail that decides whether they can get in over the sill; the success moment also carries nothing of the harbour.
findings.recommendation: Decide what a skipper needs at the harbour entrance and make that the focus of the confirmation.

findings.title: Page headings leave a single word on the last line at phone widths
findings.description: H1 'Choose a pontoon space' breaks to leave 'space' alone at 320 and 375; 'Check your mooring booking' leaves 'booking' alone at 375.
findings.impact: On the phones most skippers use, the page title is the first thing read; a stranded word makes the heading look unbalanced and the page less finished.

evidence.detail: corroborated by detector TYP-15 hits on #main > h1

findings.recommendation: Decide a heading wrap policy for narrow widths.

findings.title: Berth step heading says 'pontoon space' but lists a wall berth
findings.description: H1 'Choose a pontoon space' and label 'Pontoon spaces free on these dates' sit above four options, the last of which is 'Wall berth 2' (settles on soft mud).
findings.impact: Skippers with boats over 12 m, who must use the wall berth, may think the page does not offer one; the brief itself names 'pontoon or wall berth'.
findings.recommendation: Use one term for the choice that covers every option offered.

strengths: Copy is matter-of-fact and in skippers' own words ('Afloat at every state of the tide', 'Settles on soft mud at low water', 'The harbour office sends a text if the gate times change'); berth cards carry real decision information (size limit, tide behaviour, price).
High-contrast, legible, consistent single-column form system with a linked error summary and one primary action per step, at every captured width.
keep: Keep the plain, practical voice and the conventional one-question-per-step structure; any added identity must not reduce contrast or move controls from where skippers expect them.
not_assessable: Focus, menu behaviour, native picker on mobile, motion — stills only
Dark theme not captured (only light variants in screens.json)
